name: Alpha-lipoic acid
lead: Alpha-lipoic acid (ALA), also called lipoic acid or thioctic acid, is an organosulfur compound derived from octanoic acid. It is made in small amounts by the body and serves as an essential cofactor for several mitochondrial enzyme complexes involved in aerobic energy metabolism. It is also sold as an over-the-counter dietary supplement in the United States and as a drug in some countries, where it is marketed as an antioxidant and for glucose metabolism.[1]

In Germany it has been approved as a non-prescription drug for diabetic neuropathy since 1966.[1] Its evidence base in that condition is mixed: a 2024 Cochrane review of placebo-controlled trials lasting at least six months examined its effect as a disease-modifying agent in diabetic peripheral neuropathy,[2] and secondary sources describe its conclusion as little or no effect on symptoms.[3] Its use in anti-aging and skin-care contexts is more speculative; published reviews of antioxidants for skin health discuss it among many compounds, and no large trials of oral ALA for cosmetic outcomes were identified.[4]

In longevity and body-composition communities, ALA appears mainly as a supplement for insulin sensitivity and nutrient partitioning, discussed on forums such as T Nation. Its pharmacology, particularly the difference between racemic and R-enantiomer products and the question of whether it acts as a direct antioxidant, is itself a matter of scientific debate.[1]

(R)-enantiomer only; synthetic products are often racemic R/S

paras: Lipoic acid is a yellow solid whose structure includes a five-membered 1,2-dithiolane ring (a disulfide) attached to a pentanoic acid chain. Its reduced, open-chain form, dihydrolipoic acid (DHLA), carries two thiol groups.[1][5] Only the (R)-(+)-enantiomer occurs in nature; the (S)-(-) enantiomer exists only through chemical synthesis, first achieved in 1952.[1]

Because ordinary manufacturing produces equal amounts of both forms, most supplements are racemic R/S mixtures. The racemic form was widely used clinically in Europe and Japan from the 1950s and 1960s, even though early work recognised that the forms are not bioequivalent. Single-enantiomer production became feasible as chiral chemistry advanced, and most of the world's supply is made in China, with smaller amounts from Italy, Germany and Japan.[1] The US Pharmacopeia has published an official monograph for R/S-lipoic acid for supplement and compounding use.[1]

Lipoic acid is a covalently bound cofactor for five enzyme systems, including pyruvate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, which sit at the core of the citric acid cycle, and the glycine cleavage system.[1] The body synthesises it attached to proteins from octanoic acid made in mitochondria, so little free lipoic acid is produced. Dietary lipoic acid is mostly protein-bound and present in low amounts, with somewhat more in kidney, heart, liver, spinach, broccoli and yeast extract.[1] It enters cells through the sodium-dependent multivitamin transporter, shared with biotin and pantothenic acid, and research cited in reference works indicates these compounds compete for uptake.[1]

A frequently cited 1995 review described lipoate and dihydrolipoate as reacting with several reactive oxygen species, interacting with vitamin C and glutathione, and possibly helping recycle vitamin E.[6] Later work has complicated that picture. One reference account states that the mechanism of externally supplied ALA is controversial, that inside cells it appears to induce the oxidative stress response rather than directly scavenge radicals, and that the effect is specific to the R form; the same account notes that DHLA levels in cells are low, methylation and degradation are rapid, and radical scavenging in the test tube may not translate to cells.[1]

Preclinical studies have reported that lipoic acid can restore age-related loss of glutathione synthesis via Nrf2 transcription in rats,[7] suppress hypothalamic AMP-activated protein kinase in an animal obesity model,[8] and partly reverse memory and mitochondrial decline in old rats when combined with acetyl-L-carnitine.[9] These findings come from cell and animal models and are not by themselves evidence of effects in healthy humans.

Absorption after oral dosing is variable and is reduced by food, so product guidance generally advises taking it before or well after a meal. Peak blood levels occur roughly 30 to 60 minutes after oral intake, and it is thought to be metabolised largely in the liver.[1] A 2007 human pharmacokinetic study of the sodium salt of the R-enantiomer reported higher peak plasma concentration and bioavailability than the free acid form, approaching those from intravenous free acid.[1] Few studies have compared individual enantiomers with the racemate, and it is unclear whether twice the racemic dose substitutes for the R form.[1]

The best-established use is in symptomatic diabetic polyneuropathy. Reviews of painful diabetic neuropathy list ALA among agents used for pain management alongside gabapentinoids, SNRIs, tricyclics and capsaicin, while noting that the US FDA has approved other drugs (pregabalin, duloxetine, tapentadol and the 8% capsaicin patch) rather than ALA for this indication.[10] A 2024 review of diabetic cardiovascular autonomic neuropathy also appears among sources on diabetic nerve complications.[11] Burning mouth syndrome is another condition in which ALA supplements have been tested; a 2022 systematic review of 22 randomised trials grouped them with phytomedicines and other categories and reported that cognitive behavioural therapy, topical capsaicin, clonazepam and laser therapy showed favourable short- and long-term results.[12]

ALA is added to anti-aging supplements, multivitamins and some skin-care products on the basis of its proposed antioxidant activity.[13] A 2025 review of antioxidants for skin health covers it among numerous candidates but does not establish ALA-specific cosmetic benefit in controlled human trials.[4] Online, it is also discussed for insulin sensitivity and for taking with creatine or around training, topics in which forum posts cite small studies on glucose uptake in muscle.[14]

Diabetic neuropathy. The SYDNEY 2 trial, a multicentre double-blind placebo-controlled study in 181 diabetic patients with distal symmetric polyneuropathy in Russia and Israel, tested daily oral doses of 600, 1,200 and 1,800 mg against placebo and reported that oral ALA improved symptoms.[15] A 2023 meta-analysis of oral ALA in diabetic polyneuropathy also exists.[16] By contrast, the 2024 Cochrane review restricted itself to placebo-controlled randomised trials of at least six months, with change in Total Symptom Score at six months as its primary outcome, and states that there is no consensus about benefits and harms despite wide use.[2] Secondary summaries of that review report moderate-certainty evidence of little or no effect on symptoms and low-certainty evidence of little or no effect on impairment.[3]

Combination products. A 2024 randomised trial tested a combination of ALA and pregabalin for neuropathic pain (PAIN-CARE),[17] and another 2024 randomised trial examined a multi-ingredient product containing palmitoylethanolamide, superoxide dismutase, ALA, B vitamins, magnesium, zinc and nicotinamide over six months in diabetic neuropathy.[18] Because these are combinations, they do not isolate the effect of ALA. A 2024 randomised trial in diabetic neuropathy patients taking gabapentin or pregabalin looked at ALA and ex vivo platelet aggregation.[19]

Cardiovascular risk. A 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis of 884 randomised trials of 27 micronutrients reported that alpha-lipoic acid, among a long list of supplements, showed moderate- to high-quality evidence for reducing some cardiovascular risk factors, while the clearest reductions in clinical events were reported for omega-3 and folic acid.[20]

Other settings. A 2025 randomised placebo-controlled trial of 114 breast-surgery candidates tested a multi-ingredient supplement including ALA and found less oedema and seroma than placebo; the product contained several other active components.[21] A 2025 trial of antioxidants in IVF culture media is also listed in the literature.[22] A 2018 review cited in reference works found a small effect of ALA on body weight, and the same sources describe it as not cost-effective as a supplement for that purpose.[1] The American Cancer Society has stated that there is no reliable scientific evidence that lipoic acid prevents the development or spread of cancer, and reference works state that for mitochondrial disorders there was no good evidence of benefit as of 2012.[1]

Registered trials. ClinicalTrials.gov lists studies of ALA in radiation dermatitis in breast cancer patients (recruiting),[23] prevention of doxorubicin cardiotoxicity,[24] diabetic neuropathy,[25] progressive multiple sclerosis (racemic versus R-lipoic acid tolerability),[26] and contrast-induced kidney injury in type 2 diabetes,[27] among others. A trial in thyroid cancer was withdrawn.[28] No registered trial found on appearance outcomes such as skin ageing.

Reference sources describe ALA as generally well tolerated in clinical studies, with mild effects such as gastrointestinal upset, nausea and rash, and rare hypoglycaemia reported mainly in people using glucose-lowering drugs; data on very long-term use are limited.[1][29] One encyclopedic source advises caution in people with thiamine deficiency.[29] Forum users describe an unusual urine odour, sometimes compared to the smell after eating asparagus, and heartburn or stomach upset.[30] The toxic dose in cats is far lower than in humans or dogs and produces liver toxicity.[1] Product labels on combination homeopathic-style products that include lipoic acid advise asking a health professional if pregnant or breast-feeding.[31]

In the United States ALA and its R-form are sold as dietary supplements in capsules, tablets and liquids.[1] In Germany it is approved as a drug for diabetic neuropathy and available without prescription; intravenous ALA is not approved elsewhere in the world, according to a 2015 statement cited in reference works.[1]

subs.h: Use in looksmaxxing and bodybuilding communities
paras: No looksmax.org or Reddit material on ALA was identified; community discussion appears largely on T Nation, an evidence-leaning bodybuilding forum. Posters there describe ALA as one of several nutraceuticals that improve insulin sensitivity and recommend R-form stabilised products over racemic ones, with one poster calling the racemic form ineffective.[32] Others list it with omega-3 fats, chromium or fish oil for insulin sensitivity,[33] mention it as a post-injury nerve-regeneration supplement recommended by a practitioner,[34] or discuss small intra-workout amounts to aid glucose uptake.[35] Several report side effects such as strong urine odour.[30] Posts of this kind are personal reports and not controlled data.

timeline.event: The (S)-enantiomer of lipoic acid is first made by chemical synthesis; only the (R)-form occurs in nature.[1]
Racemic lipoic acid is widely used clinically in Europe and Japan.[1]
Germany approves lipoic acid as a drug for diabetic neuropathy.[1]
An influential review describes lipoate and dihydrolipoate as a biological antioxidant system.[6]
SYDNEY 2 randomised trial of oral ALA in diabetic polyneuropathy is published.[15]
A Cochrane review assesses ALA as a disease-modifying agent in diabetic peripheral neuropathy.[2]

lore.intro: On T Nation and similar forums, ALA is discussed as a supporting supplement for insulin sensitivity, nerve recovery and antioxidant defence rather than as an appearance compound in itself.[32][33]

claims.claim: The R-form is the only version worth taking; some users say the racemic form works less well
claims.believers: A T Nation poster argues that stabilised R-ALA improves insulin sensitivity while the racemic product most vendors sell does not.[32] Others make a similar case for the sodium R-ALA salt.[35]
claims.experts: Only the R-enantiomer occurs naturally and the forms are not bioequivalent, but few studies compare enantiomers directly and it is unclear whether doubling a racemic dose substitutes for the R form.[1]

claims.claim: ALA improves insulin sensitivity and helps with carb handling
claims.believers: T Nation users list ALA with omega-3s and chromium as supplements that raise insulin sensitivity and cite small studies of enhanced muscle glucose uptake.[33][35]
claims.experts: Reference works say ALA is marketed for glucose utilisation in metabolic disorders; a 2022 meta-analysis found moderate- to high-quality evidence for reduced cardiovascular risk factors for ALA among many micronutrients.[1][20] Evidence in healthy lifters has not been established by the cited reviews.

claims.believers: One T Nation poster reports being advised high-dose ALA along with omega-3s after a nerve-related injury, and another suggests it for nerve problems.[34][36]
claims.experts: In diabetic neuropathy the 2006 SYDNEY 2 trial reported symptom improvement,[15] while the 2024 Cochrane review of six-month or longer trials found no consensus on benefits and harms and secondary summaries report little or no effect on symptoms.[2][3] Non-diabetic nerve injury has not been established as an indication.

claims.claim: ALA is a powerful antioxidant that works by scavenging free radicals
claims.believers: Supplement marketing and forum posts treat ALA and its reduced form as a broad antioxidant that regenerates vitamins C and E and glutathione.[6]
claims.experts: Early test-tube work supports radical reactivity,[6] but a later summary says it appears to act mainly by inducing the cellular stress response and that direct scavenging in cells is little evidenced.[1]

claims.claim: ALA supports anti-aging and skin appearance
claims.believers: Anti-aging supplement formulas include ALA, reflecting a belief that it counters oxidative damage and restores glutathione with age.[13][7]
claims.experts: Evidence is from cell and rodent studies; a 2025 review of antioxidants for skin discusses oral and topical antioxidants broadly and does not establish ALA-specific benefit in human trials.[4][7]

claims.claim: ALA causes a distinctive urine smell and stomach upset
claims.believers: Forum users describe a strong odour comparable to asparagus after ALA supplements.[30]
claims.experts: Clinical reviews list nausea, gastrointestinal upset and rash as the usual effects, and encyclopedic summaries mention rare hypoglycaemia.[1][29]
